steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for our paper on making graph neural networks generalize to out-of-distribution graphs in graph-level tasks. Explain why the I.I.D. assumption breaks, how subgraph-level spurious correlations cause failures, the challenges in removing them, our StableGNN framework, and the contributions.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- GNNs and graph-level tasks
- The I.I.D. assumption and OOD shifts
- Spurious correlations between subgraphs (house/star example, Figure 1)
- Two challenges for removing subgraph-level spurious correlation
- Proposed framework: StableGNN
- Contributions

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
- GNNs and graph-level tasks
  - GNNs: powerful deep learning on graphs, many applications
  - graph-level tasks: molecular graph property prediction, scene graph classification, social network category classification
  - success due to non-linear modeling: extract info from raw graph data, encode into graph representation, data-driven
- I.I.D. assumption and OOD
  - learn GNN params on training graphs, predict on unseen testing graphs
  - fundamental assumption: I.I.D. (train/test independently sampled from identical distribution)
  - hardly satisfied in reality: data selection biases, confounder factors, other peculiarities
  - testing distribution shifts = Out-Of-Distribution (OOD) shifts -> unstable predictions
  - OGB benchmark: degeneration of 5.66% to 20% points under OOD splits (structurally different graphs in train vs test)
- Spurious correlations
  - main reason for accuracy drop under shift: spurious correlation between irrelevant features and labels
  - caused by unexpected correlations between irrelevant and relevant features for a category
  - graph-level properties determined by subgraph units (e.g., groups of atoms/chemical bonds = functional units in a molecule) -> one subgraph unit = one relevant or irrelevant feature
  - example Figure 1: label = whether graph has "house" motif; first column = testing graphs
  - GCN trained where "house" coexists with "star" in most graphs -> strongly correlated structural features -> spurious correlation of "star" with label "house"
  - second column: most important subgraph used by GCN (red, from GNNExplainer)
  - GCN uses "star" for prediction; fails on graphs without "star", or other motifs (e.g., "diamond") with "star" (Section V-A)
- Two challenges
  - (1) how to explicitly encode subgraph-level info into graph representation, so decorrelation can work on subgraph-level representation
  - (2) how to remove spurious correlation among subgraph-level representations: nodes in same subgraph unit may be correlated (e.g., 'N' and 'O' atoms in '\text{NO}_{2}' groups encoded in different dimensions) but act as a whole, stable across testing distributions -> keep interior correlations, only remove correlation between subgraph-level variables
- StableGNN
  - causal representation framework for graph: flexible representation of GNNs + causal inference's ability to distinguish spurious correlations
  - challenge 1: graph high-level variable learning module, graph pooling layer maps nearby nodes to clusters = densely-connected subgraph units; theoretical proof that cluster semantics aligned across graphs by ordered concatenation
  - challenge 2: analyze GNN degeneration in causal view; causal variable distinguishing regularizer decorrelates each high-level variable pair by learning sample weights
  - two modules jointly optimized
  - Figure 1: partials out irrelevant "star", uses relevant "house"
- Contributions
  - one of the pioneer works on OOD generalization of GNNs for graph-level tasks; key for wild non-stationary environments
  - general causal representation learning framework: high-level representation + causal variable distinguisher, invariant relationship between causal variables and labels; adoptable for various base GNNs
  - comprehensive experiments on synthetic and real-world OOD graph datasets; effectiveness, flexibility, interpretability validated

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) are powerful deep learning algorithms on graphs and they have many applications. One major type of application is prediction tasks over whole graphs, i.e., graph-level tasks, like molecular graph property prediction, scene graph classification, and social network category classification, etc. This success can be attributed to the non-linear modeling capability of GNNs, which extract useful information from raw graph data and encode it into the graph representation in a data-driven way.

The basic learning diagram of existing GNNs is to learn the GNN parameters from training graphs and then make predictions on unseen testing graphs. The most fundamental assumption that guarantees this learning diagram works is the I.I.D. hypothesis, i.e., that training and testing graphs are independently sampled from the identical distribution. But in reality this hypothesis is hardly ever satisfied because of the uncontrollable way real data is generated, such as data selection biases, confounder factors or other peculiarities. The testing distribution can have uncontrolled and unknown shifts from the training distribution, which are called Out-Of-Distribution (OOD) shifts, and this makes most GNN models fail to make stable predictions. As reported by the OGB benchmark, GNN methods have a degeneration of 5.66% to 20% points when the datasets are split according to OOD settings, i.e., when structurally different graphs are split into training and testing sets.

For general machine learning models, when there is a distribution shift, the main reason for the drop in accuracy is the spurious correlation between irrelevant features and the category labels. This kind of spurious correlation is basically caused by unexpected correlations between irrelevant features and relevant features for a given category. In the graph-level tasks we focus on in this paper, the predicted properties of graphs are usually determined by subgraph units (e.g., groups of atoms and chemical bonds which represent functional units in a molecule), so we define that one subgraph unit could be one relevant feature or irrelevant feature with the graph label. Take the classification task of the “house” motif as an example, as shown in Figure 1, where the graph is labeled by whether it has a "house" motif and the first column shows the testing graphs. The GCN model is trained on a dataset where “house” motifs coexist with “star” motifs in most training graphs. With this dataset the structural features of “house” motifs and “star” motifs are strongly correlated. This unexpected correlation leads to spurious correlations between the structural features of “star” motifs and the label “house”. The second column of Figure 1 shows a visualization of the most important subgraph the GCN uses for prediction (shown in red color and generated by GNNExplainer). So the GCN model tends to use this spurious correlation, i.e., the "star" motif, for prediction. When it meets graphs without the “star” motif, or other motifs (e.g., “diamond” motifs) together with “star” motifs, the model is likely to make false predictions (See Section V-A).

- Two challenges
  - (1) explicitly encode subgraph-level info into graph representation -> decorrelation on subgraph-level representation
  - (2) remove spurious correlation among subgraph-level representations; nodes inside one unit (e.g., 'N' and 'O' in '\text{NO}_{2}') correlated but act as a whole, stable -> only remove correlation between subgraph-level variables
- StableGNN: causal representation framework; GNN representation + causal inference distinguishing spurious correlations
  - high-level variable learning module: graph pooling layer, clusters = densely-connected subgraph units; proof of alignment by ordered concatenation
  - causal variable distinguishing regularizer: decorrelate high-level variable pairs via sample weights
  - jointly optimized; Figure 1: partials out "star", uses "house"
- Contributions: pioneer work on OOD generalization of GNNs for graph-level tasks; general causal representation learning framework for various base GNNs; experiments on synthetic and real-world OOD graph datasets

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) are powerful deep learning algorithms on graphs and they have many applications. One major type of application is prediction tasks over whole graphs, i.e., graph-level tasks, like molecular graph property prediction, scene graph classification, and social network category classification, etc. This success can be attributed to the non-linear modeling capability of GNNs, which extract useful information from raw graph data and encode it into the graph representation in a data-driven way.

The basic learning diagram of existing GNNs is to learn the GNN parameters from training graphs and then make predictions on unseen testing graphs. The most fundamental assumption that guarantees this learning diagram works is the I.I.D. hypothesis, i.e., that training and testing graphs are independently sampled from the identical distribution. But in reality this hypothesis is hardly ever satisfied because of the uncontrollable way real data is generated, such as data selection biases, confounder factors or other peculiarities. The testing distribution can have uncontrolled and unknown shifts from the training distribution, which are called Out-Of-Distribution (OOD) shifts, and this makes most GNN models fail to make stable predictions. As reported by the OGB benchmark, GNN methods have a degeneration of 5.66% to 20% points when the datasets are split according to OOD settings, i.e., when structurally different graphs are split into training and testing sets.

For general machine learning models, when there is a distribution shift, the main reason for the drop in accuracy is the spurious correlation between irrelevant features and the category labels. This kind of spurious correlation is basically caused by unexpected correlations between irrelevant features and relevant features for a given category. In the graph-level tasks we focus on in this paper, the predicted properties of graphs are usually determined by subgraph units (e.g., groups of atoms and chemical bonds which represent functional units in a molecule), so we define that one subgraph unit could be one relevant feature or irrelevant feature with the graph label. Take the classification task of the “house” motif as an example, as shown in Figure 1, where the graph is labeled by whether it has a "house" motif and the first column shows the testing graphs. The GCN model is trained on a dataset where “house” motifs coexist with “star” motifs in most training graphs. With this dataset the structural features of “house” motifs and “star” motifs are strongly correlated. This unexpected correlation leads to spurious correlations between the structural features of “star” motifs and the label “house”. The second column of Figure 1 shows a visualization of the most important subgraph the GCN uses for prediction (shown in red color and generated by GNNExplainer). So the GCN model tends to use this spurious correlation, i.e., the "star" motif, for prediction. When it meets graphs without the “star” motif, or other motifs (e.g., “diamond” motifs) together with “star” motifs, the model is likely to make false predictions (See Section V-A).

To improve the OOD generalization ability of GNNs, one important way is to make GNNs get rid of this subgraph-level spurious correlation. But this is not a trivial task, and it faces two challenges: (1) How do we explicitly encode subgraph-level information into the graph representation? Since the spurious correlation usually exists between subgraphs, we need to encode this subgraph information into the graph representation, so that a decorrelation method can be developed based on the subgraph-level representation. (2) How do we remove the spurious correlation among the subgraph-level representations? Nodes in the same type of subgraph unit may be correlated, for example the information of the ‘N’ atom and the ‘O’ atom in ‘ \text{NO}_{2} ’ groups of molecular graphs may be encoded into different dimensions of the learned embedding, but they act as an integrated whole and these correlations are stable across unseen testing distributions. So we should not remove the correlation between the interior variables of one kind of subgraph and we only need to remove the spurious correlation between subgraph-level variables.

To deal with these two challenges, we propose a new causal representation framework for graphs, called StableGNN, which uses both the flexible representation ability of GNNs and the ability of causal inference methods to distinguish spurious correlations. For the first challenge, we propose a graph high-level variable learning module that uses a graph pooling layer to map nearby nodes to a set of clusters, where each cluster is one densely-connected subgraph unit of the original graph. We also prove theoretically that the semantic meanings of the clusters are aligned across graphs by an ordered concatenation operation. Given the aligned high-level variables, for the second challenge we analyze the degeneration of GNNs from a causal view and propose a new causal variable distinguishing regularizer which decorrelates each pair of high-level variables by learning a set of sample weights. The two modules are optimized jointly in our framework. Also, as shown in Figure 1, StableGNN can effectively partial out the irrelevant subgraphs (i.e., the “star” motif) and use the truly relevant subgraphs (i.e., the “house” motif) for predictions.

The main contributions of the paper are:

- To our best knowledge, we are one of the pioneer works that study the OOD generalization problem of GNNs for graph-level tasks, which is a key direction for applying GNNs in wild non-stationary environments.

- We propose a general causal representation learning framework for GNNs, which jointly learns the high-level representation together with the causal variable distinguisher, and which can learn an invariant relationship between the graph causal variables and the labels. Our framework is general and can be adopted for various base GNN models to help them get rid of spurious correlations.

- We conduct comprehensive experiments on synthetic datasets and on real-world OOD graph datasets. The results validate the effectiveness, flexibility and interpretability of the proposed framework.

For the first challenge, we propose a graph high-level variable learning module that employs a graph pooling layer to map nearby nodes to a set of clusters, each of which is one densely-connected subgraph unit of the original graph. Moreover, we theoretically prove that the semantic meanings of the clusters are aligned across graphs by an ordered concatenation operation. Given the aligned high-level variables, to overcome the second challenge, we analyze the degeneration of GNNs from a causal view and propose a novel causal variable distinguishing regularizer that decorrelates each high-level variable pair by learning a set of sample weights. The two modules are jointly optimized in our framework. Furthermore, as shown in Figure 1, StableGNN can effectively partial out the irrelevant subgraphs (i.e., the “star” motif) and leverage the truly relevant subgraphs (i.e., the “house” motif) for predictions.

In summary, the major contributions of the paper are as follows:

- • To our best knowledge, we are one of the pioneer works studying the OOD generalization problem of GNNs for graph-level tasks, which is a key direction for applying GNNs to wild non-stationary environments.

- • We propose a general causal representation learning framework for GNNs that jointly learns the high-level representation with the causal variable distinguisher, which can learn an invariant relationship between the graph causal variables and the labels. Our framework is general enough to be adopted for various base GNN models to help them get rid of spurious correlations.

- • Comprehensive experiments are conducted on both synthetic datasets and real-world OOD graph datasets, and the effectiveness, flexibility and interpretability of the proposed framework are well validated.
